title: Configuration and secrets
summary: One image for every environment: configure with environment variables, and keep secrets out of images.

steps.title: Build once, configure per environment
body: The image you tested is the image you ship. It must not be rebuilt for staging or production; **configuration comes from the environment** at run time (one of the "twelve-factor app" rules).
.NET reads environment variables on top of `appsettings.json`, and `__` maps to `:`:
Keys are case-insensitive. Node apps read `process.env.X`; the idea is the same everywhere.

steps.prompt: Match each environment variable to the .NET configuration key it sets.

steps.title: Secrets never go in the image
body: Anyone who can pull an image can read **every layer**, and `docker history` shows every instruction:
ENV DB_PASSWORD=hunter2              # baked into the image config forever
ARG NPM_TOKEN                        # build args show up in docker history
COPY .env .                          # the file is in a layer, even if a later RUN deletes it

- **At run time**, inject secrets from the platform: Compose/Swarm `secrets:` (mounted as files under `/run/secrets/`), Kubernetes Secrets, a cloud key vault. Environment variables are acceptable for many teams, but files are not visible in `docker inspect`.
- **At build time** (a private package feed token), use a BuildKit secret mount, which exists only during that one `RUN` and is never written to a layer:

steps.prompt: A Dockerfile has `COPY .npmrc .`, then `RUN npm ci && rm .npmrc`. Is the token safe?
options: No: the COPY layer still contains .npmrc; deleting it later only hides it in the final filesystem
Yes: the file was deleted before the image was finished
Yes, as long as the image is pushed to a private registry
No, but only because npm logs the token
steps.explain: Layers are additive. Use `RUN --mount=type=secret,...` so the file never lands in a layer.

steps.prompt: Does the secret end up readable by someone who pulls the image?
Use a private NuGet feed during `dotnet restore` without leaving the credentials in any layer.
Which configuration key does a .NET app see for this variable? Type the key.

steps.title: Move a password from an env var to a secret
prompt: This terminal has a **real Docker Engine** with Compose. `~/billing/compose.yaml` passes the database password as
the environment variable `DB_PASSWORD` (from `~/billing/.env`). Anyone who can run `docker inspect` can read it.
1. the password comes from a Compose **secret** read from the file `~/billing/db_password.txt`, and the container
finds it through `DB_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db_password` (the app supports that convention);
2. no `DB_PASSWORD` is left in the container's environment (and the old `.env` line is gone);
3. while you are there, set the .NET-style setting `Logging:LogLevel:Default` to `Warning` through the environment.
`docker compose up -d` from `~/billing`; `docker compose logs billing` says where the password came from.

checks.name: the app loaded the password from the secret file
checks.cmd: cd ~/billing && docker compose logs --no-log-prefix billing | grep 'password loaded'
checks.fail: The app did not load the password from `/run/secrets/db_password`.

checks.name: no DB_PASSWORD in the container's environment
checks.cmd: c=$(cd ~/billing && docker compose ps -q billing); test -n "$c" && ! docker inspect -f '{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}' $c | grep -q '^DB_PASSWORD=' && ! grep -q '^DB_PASSWORD=' ~/billing/.env 2>/dev/null
checks.fail: `DB_PASSWORD` is still in the container's environment or in `.env`: `docker inspect` shows env vars to anyone with Docker access.

checks.name: the secret is declared from db_password.txt
checks.cmd: cd ~/billing && docker compose config --format json | jq -r '.secrets.db_password.file'
checks.fail: Declare `secrets: db_password: file: ./db_password.txt` at the top level, and list it under the service.

checks.name: the log level reaches the app
checks.cmd: cd ~/billing && docker compose logs --no-log-prefix billing | grep 'log level'
checks.fail: The app does not see `Logging:LogLevel:Default=Warning`. In environment variables `:` is written `__`.

hints: Top level `secrets: {db_password: {file: ./db_password.txt}}`; under the service `secrets: [db_password]` mounts it at `/run/secrets/db_password`.
Put the password into `db_password.txt` first (it is in `.env` now), then delete the `.env` line.
steps.explain: Environment variables leak: `docker inspect`, `/proc/1/environ`, crash dumps and child processes all see them. A secret is a file mounted at `/run/secrets/NAME`, read only by the app that needs it; the `*_FILE` convention (used by the official postgres, mysql and many other images) is how apps take it. The `__` trick is how .NET maps `Logging:LogLevel:Default` to an environment variable, since `:` is not allowed in every shell.
